questions.text: How many rows will a truth table have if it involves 4 propositions?
questions.explanation: The module states: 'In general, a truth table involving "n" propositions p₁, p₂, ..., pₙ contains 2ⁿ possible combinations of truth values.' For n = 4, 2⁴ = 16 rows. Option A (4) is just n. Option B (8) is 2³. Option D (32) is 2⁵.

questions.text: What is the correct reading of the expression $p \wedge q \Rightarrow r$?
questions.explanation: The module states: 'Whenever "\vee" or "\wedge" occur with "\Rightarrow" or "\Leftrightarrow", we shall assume that "\vee" or "\wedge" is applied first, and then "\Rightarrow" or "\Leftrightarrow" is then applied. For example, p ∧ q ⇒ r means (p ∧ q) ⇒ r.' Option A is incorrect because it applies ⇒ before ∧. Option C and D are incorrect bracket placements.

questions.text: Suppose p, q, r, and s have truth values T, F, F, T. What is the truth value of $(p \vee q) \Rightarrow (r \Leftrightarrow \neg s)$?
options: D) Depends on the order of operations
questions.explanation: Evaluate step-by-step: p ∨ q = T ∨ F = T. ¬s = ¬T = F. r ⇔ ¬s = F ⇔ F = T. Finally, T ⇒ T = T. Option B would be true if the implication was F ⇒ T. Option C is incorrect because the values are fully determined. Option D is incorrect because the order is fixed by convention.

questions.text: Given $p \equiv T$ and $q \equiv F$, what is the truth value of $\neg p \land q$?
questions.explanation: First, ¬p = ¬T = F. Then, F ∧ F = F. Option A would be true only if both components were true. Option C is incorrect because the values are fully determined.

questions.text: What is the truth value of the compound proposition $(p \Rightarrow q) \Leftrightarrow (\neg p \vee q)$?
options: C) Depends on p and q
D) Only true when p is true
questions.explanation: This is the definition of logical equivalence for implication. Using a truth table: If p=T, q=T: (T⇒T) ⇔ (F∨T) = T ⇔ T = T. If p=T, q=F: (T⇒F) ⇔ (F∨F) = F ⇔ F = T. If p=F, q=T: (F⇒T) ⇔ (T∨T) = T ⇔ T = T. If p=F, q=F: (F⇒F) ⇔ (T∨F) = T ⇔ T = T. It is always true.

questions.text: Let $P \equiv (p \land q) \Rightarrow p$. Which of the following is true about $P$?
options: C) It depends on p and q.
D) It is only true when p is false.
questions.explanation: Evaluate the truth table: If p=T, q=T: (T∧T)⇒T = T⇒T = T. If p=T, q=F: (T∧F)⇒T = F⇒T = T. If p=F, q=T: (F∧T)⇒F = F⇒F = T. If p=F, q=F: (F∧F)⇒F = F⇒F = T. Thus, P is a tautology. Option B is incorrect because the statement is never false. Option C is incorrect because the truth value does not change. Option D is incorrect because it is true for all cases.

questions.text: If $p \Leftrightarrow q$ is true, what is the truth value of $\neg p \Leftrightarrow \neg q$?
options: D) Depends on the value of p
questions.explanation: If p ⇔ q is true, then p and q have the same truth value. Therefore, ¬p and ¬q will also have the same truth value. When two propositions have the same truth value, their bi-implication is true. Option B would be true if p and q had different truth values. Option C and D are incorrect because the truth value is fully determined.

questions.text: Suppose $p \Rightarrow q$ is false. What can you conclude about the truth values of p and q?
options: A) p is true and q is true.
B) p is true and q is false.
C) p is false and q is true.
D) p is false and q is false.
questions.correct_answer: B) p is true and q is false.
questions.explanation: The module states: 'p ⇒ q is false if and only if p is true and q is false.' Option A would make the implication true. Option C would make the implication true (by vacuous truth). Option D would make the implication true (by vacuous truth).

questions.text: Which of the following is logically equivalent to $p \Rightarrow q$?
questions.explanation: The module states: 'As we observed from example 1.7, the conditional p ⇒ q and its contrapositive ¬q ⇒ ¬p are equivalent.' Option A is the converse (not equivalent). Option B is the inverse (not equivalent). Option D is the biconditional (not equivalent).

questions.text: Evaluate the truth value of the compound proposition $(p \Rightarrow (q \land r)) \lor (\neg p \land q)$ when $p \equiv F, q \equiv T, r \equiv F$.
options: D) Depends on the order of operations
questions.explanation: Evaluate step-by-step: q ∧ r = T ∧ F = F. p ⇒ (q ∧ r) = F ⇒ F = T. ¬p = ¬F = T. ¬p ∧ q = T ∧ T = T. Finally, (p ⇒ (q ∧ r)) ∨ (¬p ∧ q) = T ∨ T = T. Option B would be true only if both sides were false. Option C is incorrect because values are fully determined. Option D is incorrect because the order of operations is fixed.
